prompt_c2:
You are a streetscape inventory annotator. Look ONLY at the uploaded streetscape image.
Return JSON ONLY. No markdown, no commentary, no reasoning.
 Task: record what is visible in the scene. Do not score, do not give design advice.
 Schema:
{
"road_type": "highway|arterial|neighborhood_street|alley|plaza|unclear",
"elements": {
"sidewalk": "true|false|unclear",
"bike_lane": "true|false|unclear",
"seating": "true|false|unclear",
"shade_trees": "none|few|many|unclear",
"curb_ramp": "true|false|unclear",
"tactile_paving": "true|false|unclear",
"pedestrian_crossing": "true|false|unclear",
"street_lighting": "true|false|unclear",
"greenery": "none|low|medium|high|unclear",
"vehicle_traffic": "none|light|heavy|unclear",
"bus_stop": "true|false|unclear"
},
"issues": ["no_seating", "little_shade", "no_bike_lane", "poor_accessibility", "narrow_sidewalk", "no_crossing", "high_traffic_exposure"],
"brief": "One or two English sentences describing the visible street scene."
}
 Rules:
- If an element is not clearly visible, use "unclear". Do not guess.
- "issues" may only list problems that are visible. Use [] if none.
- "brief" must mention concrete objects (sidewalk, trees, lanes, benches, ramps, etc.).

passages.text: and acceptance criteria shall be formulated in accordance with design requirements and site conditions. 1.1.5 Maintenance Key Points 1. Sidewalks shall be firm and level, with no cracks, missing bricks, damage, or other defects; joint widths shall be uniform and joints fully filled. All manhole covers shall be flush with the sidewalk elevation and in good condition, and their strength must meet sidewalk traffic requirements. 2. Sidewalks must have a base course and bedding course of sufficient strength. For settlement, breakage, or damage caused by insufficient base-course strength, the base course shall first be reinforced before the surface blocks are repaved. 3. To ensure safe pedestrian passage in rain and snow, the longitudinal slope of sidewalk ramps shall be ≤1:20. Smooth-surfaced ramp slabs shall be treated with anti-slip measures. Ramps that do not meet the requirements shall be demolished and reconstructed during rectification. 1.2 At-Grade Crossing System 1.2.1 Crossing at At-Grade Intersections 1. Basic Principles A. The slow-traffic organization for pedestrians and non-motor vehicles within grade-separated interchange areas shall be continuous, safe, and convenient, and should be arranged at ground level to avoid pedestrians and non-motor vehicles having to go up and down or increasing detour distances. 2. Quality Enhancement A. Reducing crossing distance Reducing the curb radius at intersections can effectively lower turning speeds, shorten pedestrian crossing distances, and enlarge pedestrian waiting areas. The facility strip or green belt along the roadside may also be appropriately used to create a pedestrian stopping space. Table 1.2-1 Recommended Curb Radius Values | Road class | Recommended curb radius (m) | |---|---:| | Main and secondary arterial roads | 5–10 | | Branch roads | 5–8 | Note: For exclusive right-turn lanes with traffic islands, the recommended curb radius is 8–10 m. Figure 1.2-1 Reducing Road Curb Radius B. Secondary crossing refuge island When the pedestrian or bicycle crossing traverses more than 4 lanes of two-way motor vehicle traffic, or when the crossing length exceeds 16 m, a secondary crossing refuge island shall be set in the center of the road. The island width shall not be less than 2 m, and in difficult circumstances not less than 1.5 m. On roads with a median strip (or where lane width can be reduced), pedestrian crossings on signal-free sections shall be provided with a “Z”-shaped secondary crossing refuge island. The refuge island length shall not be less than 8 m, and corresponding guardrails shall be installed. Figure 1.2-2 Schematic Diagram of a “Z”-Shaped Secondary Crossing Refuge Island I C. All-direction cross intersection For intersections surrounded by relatively dense commercial facilities and heavy pedestrian flows, an “all-direction cross intersection” may be used as appropriate. This not only improves pedestrian crossing efficiency, but also prevents interference between pedestrians and motor vehicles. D. Improving the experience of non-motor vehicle crossings Intersections with large non-motor vehicle crossing volumes should be equipped with dedicated non-motor vehicle signal lights. At branch-road intersections with heavy non-motor vehicle traffic, explore moving the non-motor vehicle crossing waiting area in front of the motor vehicle stop line and granting an early green signal priority. Road User Type

- Drivers

Selected Indicators:
Justice; Safety; Livability; Sustainability; Aesthetics; Comfort; Walkability
 1. Evaluation Dimensions
Justice: Analyze whether the environment fairly distributes spatial resources, including Equity (rationality of asset distribution), Fairness (non-discriminatory rules), and Accessibility (barrier-free physical design).
Comfort: Analyze physical perception at a micro-scale, including Thermal Comfort (shade/vegetation), Physical Comfort (paving/seating), and Psychological Comfort (noise/crowding).
Core Indicators: Safety, Livability, Sustainability, Aesthetics, Walkability, and Bikeability.
 2. Persona Perspective Requirements:
The analysis must strictly adhere to the persona's characteristics. For example:
Persons with Disabilities: Focus on curb ramps, continuity of tactile paving (blind tracks), and physical obstacles.
Elderly: Focus on resting facilities, slope gradients, and summer shade.
Teenagers: Focus on traffic calming measures and social surveillance (Eyes on the street).
 3. How to use the image vs retrieved knowledge:
- The IMAGE is the primary evidence. Score only what is visible or reasonably inferable from the photo.
- Section 6 provides retrieved guidelines and research. Use them to interpret the image (what the scene should provide for this persona/indicators), not to invent objects that are not in the photo.
- If retrieved text conflicts with the image, trust the image and say so in the explanation.
- Explanations must cite specific visible objects (benches, ramps, tree shade, lane markings, etc.). When a guideline is used, briefly connect it to those objects.

Purpose of Formulation Under the macro guidance of the “General Provisions,” these Detailed Rules aim at the refined construction of Suzhou’s urban roads, and are expanded and implemented from four directions: human-oriented, quality-oriented, distinctive, and intelligent. They interpret the refined construction of Suzhou’s urban roads in the form of colorful labels, and create urban colorful roads unique to Suzhou. ➢ Human-oriented: Starting from the users of Suzhou’s urban roads, and taking the public’s experience of urban road space as the benchmark, fully consider the comfort, safety, and convenience of public activities, and realize the value shift from “vehicle-centered” to “people-centered.” ➢ Quality-oriented: Vigorously improve the travel quality of people and vehicle traffic in Suzhou, and emphasize the public space function of roads. Appropriately raise the standards for urban road design, construction, and maintenance, extend road service life, and improve users’ comfort of experience. Reflect a road construction level of high appearance and high standards, with attention to detail and control. ➢ Distinctive: Adapt measures to local conditions, and through the embedding of Suzhou-style elements and the creation of road characteristic scenes, highlight Suzhou’s distinctive urban character of integration between tradition and modernity, so that urban roads become an important carrier and display space for the “Jiangnan culture” brand, and continue the city’s historical and cultural lineage. ➢ Intelligent: Deploy intelligent sensing devices along the roadside, together with cloud service platforms, computing and communication facilities, and through data technologies such as autonomous driving and vehicle-road coordination, realize a travel experience of deep interaction among people, vehicles, and road space, assist safe driving and autonomous driving, and create demonstration roads with Suzhou’s smart-city characteristics. 2. Sidewalks shall be firm and level, with no cracks, missing bricks, damage, or other defects; joint widths shall be uniform and joints fully filled. All manhole covers shall be flush with the sidewalk elevation and in good condition, and their strength must meet sidewalk traffic requirements. 2. Sidewalks must have a base course and bedding course of sufficient strength. For settlement, breakage, or damage caused by insufficient base-course strength, the base course shall first be reinforced before the surface blocks are repaved. 3. To ensure safe pedestrian passage in rain and snow, the longitudinal slope of sidewalk ramps shall be ≤1:20. Smooth-surfaced ramp slabs shall be treated with anti-slip measures. Ramps that do not meet the requirements shall be demolished and reconstructed during rectification. 1.2 At-Grade Crossing System 1.2.1 Crossing at At-Grade Intersections 1. Basic Principles A. The slow-traffic organization for pedestrians and non-motor vehicles within grade-separated interchange areas shall be continuous, safe, and convenient, and should be arranged at ground level to avoid pedestrians and non-motor vehicles having to go up and down or increasing detour distances. 2. Quality Enhancement A. Reducing crossing distance Reducing the curb radius at intersections can effectively lower turning speeds, shorten pedestrian crossing distances, and enlarge pedestrian waiting areas. The facility strip or green belt along the roadside may also be appropriately used to create a pedestrian stopping space. Table 1.2-1 Recommended Curb Radius Values | Road class | Recommended curb radius (m) | |---|---:| | Main and secondary arterial roads | 5–10 | | Branch roads | 5–8 | Note: For exclusive right-turn lanes with traffic islands, the recommended curb radius is 8–10 m. Figure 1.2-1 Reducing Road Curb Radius B. Secondary crossing refuge island When the pedestrian or bicycle crossing traverses more than 4 lanes of two-way motor vehicle traffic, or when the crossing length exceeds 16 m, a secondary crossing refuge island shall be set in the center of the road. The island width shall not be less than 2 m, and in difficult circumstances not less than 1.5 m. On roads with a median strip (or where lane width can be reduced), pedestrian crossings on signal-free sections shall be provided with a “Z”-shaped secondary crossing refuge island. The refuge island length shall not be less than 8 m, and corresponding guardrails shall be installed. Figure 1.2-2 Schematic Diagram of a “Z”-Shaped Secondary Crossing Refuge Island I C. All-direction cross intersection For intersections surrounded by relatively dense commercial facilities and heavy pedestrian flows, an “all-direction cross intersection” may be used as appropriate. This not only improves pedestrian crossing efficiency, but also prevents interference between pedestrians and motor vehicles. D. Improving the experience of non-motor vehicle crossings Intersections with large non-motor vehicle crossing volumes should be equipped with dedicated non-motor vehicle signal lights.
